title: Checkbox and Radio Styling
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of checkbox and radio styling.
Apply one appropriate technique to a small Tailwind CSS example.
Verify the expected result and identify a common failure mode.

content.intro: In this lesson, focus on checkbox and radio styling and connect it to the way Tailwind CSS generates and applies utility styles.
content.why_it_matters: Checkbox and Radio Styling matters because interface appearance should reflect actual state while remaining understandable to keyboard, touch and assistive-technology users.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: The source curriculum highlights: Native control appearance; Checked states; Accent colors; Custom visual treatments; Maintaining accessible interaction. Treat these as practical decisions rather than a list to memorize: identify the intended behavior, choose the smallest suitable utility or directive, and inspect what the browser receives.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Checkbox and Radio Styling
content_blocks.expected_output: A required email field is explicitly labeled and keeps a visible focus state.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Start with the example, change one decision related to checkbox and radio styling, then compare the outcome. In a Tailwind-enabled project, confirm the generated CSS exists; class strings alone do not make styles available without a configured build.

content_blocks.title: Version and compatibility note
content_blocks.text: This course prioritizes Tailwind CSS v4. Confirm your installed version and use its matching official guide. Snippets using v3 directives or configuration are labelled as legacy and should not be mixed blindly with v4 syntax.

content.task: Create a minimal example demonstrating checkbox and radio styling. Include a before/after comparison and explain why the chosen utility, variant or directive is appropriate.
task_acceptance_criteria: Demonstrate at least one decision tied to checkbox and radio styling.
Keep the example easy to inspect, with complete utility names.
Test the outcome and document one limitation or environment assumption.
hints: Identify which listed syllabus topic is most important to checkbox and radio styling.
Change one utility, token, variant or configuration setting at a time.
Inspect generated CSS and computed styles before changing unrelated code.
content.expected_output: A required email field is explicitly labeled and keeps a visible focus state.
troubleshooting: If no style appears, verify the package, CSS import and build-tool integration before changing the HTML.
If only a state or breakpoint style fails, check the full class token, source detection, condition and computed CSS.
For a framework snippet, import the stylesheet through its supported entry point and consult the current official guide.
common_mistakes: Applying checkbox and radio styling without checking generated styles or browser behavior.
Mixing Tailwind v3 and v4 setup examples without a migration plan.
Treating visual appearance as a substitute for semantic markup, keyboard usability or actual component behavior.
summary: Checkbox and Radio Styling is one part of a predictable utility-first styling workflow.
Keep examples small, test the built interface and use version-matched documentation.
